body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Adherence to risk-tailored antiemetic prophylaxis in ambulatory surgery: an observational study","authors":"Kowalski-Mensah J, Oduya-Bright L, Svensson-Park A","year":2018,"venue":"Orrinford Journal of Perioperative Practice","doi":"10.5555/ojpp.2018.0412","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the antiemetic prophylaxis given with that recommended by a risk-tailored protocol in consecutive adults undergoing ambulatory surgery at two hospitals. Across 3,400 ambulatory surgery patients, prophylaxis matched the risk-tailored protocol in 52 percent. Under-prophylaxis was most common in patients with the highest risk scores, who received fewer agents than recommended in 38 percent of cases, while over-prophylaxis was most common in low-risk patients. Adherence varied more between anaesthetists than between surgical specialties. Risk scores were reconstructed from records, which may have misclassified some patients. A protocol alone did not ensure that prophylaxis matched risk."},{"title":"Under-prophylaxis and nausea or vomiting requiring rescue treatment after day surgery: a case-control analysis","authors":"Ferreira-Nakashima D, Achebe-Holm R","year":2021,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Anaesthesia Reports","doi":"10.5555/kar.2021.0078","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified 214 day surgery patients who needed rescue antiemetic treatment in recovery and 428 controls from the same operating lists, and read their anaesthetic records to classify prophylaxis against the unit protocol. Under-prophylaxis was associated with nausea or vomiting requiring rescue treatment (adjusted odds ratio 1.8, 95 percent CI 1.2 to 2.7) after adjustment for risk score, duration of surgery and opioid dose. Over-prophylaxis was not associated with fewer rescue treatments. Record readers were not blinded to case status, and the protocol changed during the study period. The findings support checking adherence as a target for improvement."},{"title":"Recovery unit nausea logs as a source of outcome data: agreement with nurse observation","authors":"Mbatha-Carlsson T, Rao-Whitfield P","year":2016,"venue":"Harthill Recovery Nursing Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared entries in a recovery unit nausea log with direct observation by research nurses for 480 adults after day surgery. Recovery unit nausea logs captured 87 percent of rescue antiemetic treatments seen by nurse observers, and almost all missed entries occurred during busy periods at the end of the day. Nausea that did not lead to treatment was captured far less reliably. Entries were accurate for the drug and the time given. The log is a reasonable source for rescue treatment as an outcome but not for nausea severity. The study took place in one unit with an established logging culture."},{"title":"Risk-tailored versus fixed antiemetic prophylaxis for adults having surgery: a review of comparative studies","authors":"Delacroix-Osei M, Lindgren-Adeyemi S, Tanaka-Frost E, Holloway-Nkemelu B","year":2023,"venue":"Vellmar Anaesthesia Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/vas.2023.0156","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 19 comparative studies of risk-tailored and fixed antiemetic prophylaxis in adults having surgery under general anaesthesia. Risk-tailored prophylaxis reduced the incidence of nausea and vomiting in high-risk patients compared with fixed single-agent regimens, while low-risk patients received fewer drugs with similar outcomes. Benefits depended on adherence, which was reported in only seven studies and was often below 60 percent. Few studies reported discharge outcomes after day surgery. Most studies were before-after comparisons with moderate to high risk of bias, and definitions of nausea and vomiting varied widely."},{"title":"Unplanned overnight admission after day surgery: causes and the contribution of nausea and vomiting","authors":"Quinn-Adebayo F, Solberg-Marsh K","year":2019,"venue":"Orrinford Journal of Perioperative Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed all unplanned overnight admissions after day surgery in three units over one year. Of 312 unplanned admissions, 31 percent were attributed to nausea and vomiting, 24 percent to pain and 18 percent to surgical complications. Admissions for nausea were more common after gynaecological laparoscopy and in patients who received opioids in recovery. Units differed in how they recorded the reason for admission, and the attribution was made by the discharging nurse. Reducing nausea and vomiting could reduce unplanned admissions substantially, but the proportion depends on local case mix."},{"title":"Over-prophylaxis with antiemetics and sedation delaying discharge after day surgery","authors":"Brennan-Iqbal O, Varga-Lund C","year":2025,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Anaesthesia Reports","doi":"10.5555/kar.2025.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined whether giving more antiemetic agents than recommended by the risk score affected recovery after day surgery in 1,860 adults. Giving more antiemetic agents than the risk score indicated was associated with sedation that delayed discharge in 6 percent of patients, compared with 2 percent of patients whose prophylaxis matched the score. The difference was largest when a sedating antihistamine was added. Rescue treatment rates were similar in the two groups. The analysis could not fully separate the effect of extra antiemetics from that of the conditions that prompted anaesthetists to give them."}]}
